title: In the Community
goals: Talk about possible future situations and their results with if + present, will.
Ask for information politely with noun clauses: Do you know where...? Can you tell me what time...?
Give your opinion with I think that... and I don't know how much...
Say when things will happen with when, before, after and as soon as + present.
Understand a transport service alert and talk about getting to work.
Describe a community problem and suggest solutions in writing.

learn.title: Future real conditional: if + present, will
learn.html:
Use the future real conditional to talk about a possible situation in the future and its result. The if clause says the condition. The main clause says what will happen.

if clause (present)result clause (will + base verb)
If it rains on Saturday,we will move the festival indoors.
If more neighbors help,the clean-up will finish early.
If you don't register,you won't get a ticket.
  • The two parts can change places: We will cancel the event if it rains. With the if clause first, we use a comma.
  • Questions: What will you do if the bus is late?
  • In the if clause we use the simple present, even if the meaning is about the future.

watch.wrong: If it will rain, we will cancel the picnic.
watch.right: If it rains, we will cancel the picnic.
watch.why: Do not use will in the if clause. Use the simple present.

watch.wrong: If you come early, you would get a good seat.
watch.right: If you come early, you will get a good seat.
watch.why: For a possible future situation, use will in the result clause.

watch.wrong: If she doesn't come, we not will start.
watch.right: If she doesn't come, we won't start.
watch.why: The negative of will is won't (will not).

watch.wrong: We will help you if you will ask us.
watch.right: We will help you if you ask us.
watch.why: No will after if, even when the if clause comes second.

learn.title: Noun clauses: I think that... / Do you know where...?
learn.html:
A noun clause is a small sentence inside a bigger sentence. We use it after phrases such as I think, I know, I don't know, Do you know...? and Can you tell me...?

Direct questionNoun clause
Where is the community center?Do you know where the community center is?
What time does the meeting start?I don't know what time the meeting starts.
How much does the ticket cost?Can you tell me how much the ticket costs?
  • In a noun clause the word order is like a statement: subject + verb. We do not use do / does / did and we do not put the verb before the subject.
  • After I think, I believe and I know, we can use that: I think that the garden is a great idea. In conversation, that is often left out.
  • For yes/no questions use if: Do you know if the library is open?

watch.wrong: Do you know where is the post office?
watch.right: Do you know where the post office is?
watch.why: In a noun clause the subject goes before the verb.

watch.wrong: I don't know what time does the event start.
watch.right: I don't know what time the event starts.
watch.why: No does in a noun clause. Use the verb with -s.

watch.wrong: Can you tell me how much costs the ticket?
watch.right: Can you tell me how much the ticket costs?
watch.why: Use subject + verb: the ticket costs.

watch.wrong: Do you know if is the library open?
watch.right: Do you know if the library is open?
watch.why: After if, the order is subject + verb as well.

learn.title: Future time clauses: when, before, after, as soon as
learn.html:
A future time clause tells when something will happen. It starts with when, before, after, as soon as or until. The time clause uses the simple present. The main clause uses will (or be going to).

Time clause (present)Main clause (future)
When the bus arrives,we will go to the market.
Before I leave home,I will check the service alert.
After the festival ends,the volunteers will clean the park.
As soon as I get to work,I will call you.
  • The clauses can change places: I will call you as soon as I get to work. Use a comma only when the time clause is first.
  • As soon as means "immediately after".
  • Never use will directly after when, before, after, as soon as or until.

watch.wrong: When I will arrive, I will call you.
watch.right: When I arrive, I will call you.
watch.why: Use the simple present in the time clause, not will.

watch.wrong: I will send the message as soon as I will get home.
watch.right: I will send the message as soon as I get home.
watch.why: No will after as soon as.

watch.wrong: After the meeting will finish, we will have lunch.
watch.right: After the meeting finishes, we will have lunch.
watch.why: Time clause: simple present with the -s for he / she / it.

watch.wrong: Before we leave, we call a taxi. (a future plan)
watch.right: Before we leave, we will call a taxi.
watch.why: The main clause needs will for a future action.

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• Are you going to the festival on Saturday? — asking about a community event.
  • I'd love to come! / Sorry, I can't make it. — accepting or declining an invitation.
  • Can I help? / We need more volunteers. — offering and asking for help.
  • Do you know what time it starts? / Could you tell me where it is? — asking politely for information.
  • How do you get to work? — I usually take the bus. — talking about transport.
  • Do you know which bus goes downtown? — asking for directions at a stop.
  • I'll be late. There's a delay on the metro. — explaining why you are late.

A short service alert looks like this: Attention, passengers: Line 2 is out of service between Central and Park stations due to a technical problem. Shuttle buses are available. Normal service will resume as soon as the repairs are finished. We apologize for the inconvenience.

write.prompt: Write a problem-solution essay (120 to 160 words) about a problem in your neighborhood or city (for example trash, traffic, noise or a lack of parks). Describe the problem, give two solutions, and say what will happen if people follow them. Use at least two if + will sentences and one time clause. Opening: One big problem in my neighborhood is...
checklist: A clear problem and two solutions
At least two sentences with if + present, will
One sentence with when, before, after or as soon as + present
One noun clause (I think that... / I don't know where...)
No will after if or when
write.model:
One big problem in my neighborhood is trash in the streets. After the Sunday market, there are bags, bottles and boxes everywhere. I think that this problem makes people feel unhappy about the place where they live. It also attracts rats and bad smells.

There are two simple solutions. First, the city can put more trash cans near the market. If there are more trash cans, people will use them. Second, neighbors can organize a clean-up day every month. When volunteers work together, the work will be easy and fast. Children can also join, and they will learn to take care of the community.

If we do these things, the neighborhood will be cleaner and safer. As soon as people see a clean street, they will want to keep it clean. I don't know how much it will cost, but I am sure that it is worth the effort.

Hello, neighbors!

We are organizing a clean-up day in our park this Saturday at nine in the morning. We will meet next to the main gate. We need volunteers, so please bring gloves and a bag if you can. If it rains, we will do it next Saturday instead. We will have water and fruit for everyone.

Do you know someone who wants to help? Please tell your friends and family. Could you tell me how many people will come? I would like to buy enough food. Please reply to this message as soon as you can.

Thank you for helping our neighborhood!

Laura

reading.title: A Garden for Everyone
reading.intro: Read the text about a community garden and answer.
paragraphs: Three years ago, the empty lot behind the Hidalgo Street market was full of trash. The neighbors complained about the smell and the rats, but nobody knew what to do. Then a retired teacher, Mrs. Lupita Ramos, said, "If we clean this place, we can grow vegetables here." At first, many people laughed at the idea.

Only six people came to help on the first Saturday. They collected bags of trash, moved heavy stones and asked the city for permission to use the land. The city agreed, but it gave them one rule: if the neighbors take care of the garden, they can keep it. Today more than sixty families work there, and the lot is full of green plants.

Each family has a small plot and pays 100 pesos a year for water and tools. They grow tomatoes, chiles, beans and herbs. They also make compost from food waste, so they don't need to buy expensive fertilizer. Every Saturday morning, a group of volunteers teaches children how to plant seeds and why healthy food is important.

The garden has changed more than the neighborhood's food. People who never spoke before now share tools, recipes and stories. An older man, Mr. Ortiz, says that he always knows where to find fresh vegetables, and he also knows who needs help. When someone is sick, the others water that person's plot. Teenagers come too, and many of them say that the garden is the best place to relax after school.

There are problems, too. Last summer there was not enough rain, and the water bill was very high. Mrs. Ramos thinks that the garden needs a rain tank. The group is organizing a fundraiser: as soon as they collect 20,000 pesos, they will buy the tank. They will hold a small festival next month, and after the festival ends, they will count the money. "If everyone brings a friend, we will reach our goal," she says with a smile.

Anything you like. Before you come, please write your name on the list at the center.
We'll do it today. Thanks, Mrs. Vega!
